Transport a fitted backward joint model to a new population

Source: R/transportBJM.R
transportBJM.Rd

Experimental. Adapts a survival sub-model fitted in one population (the source, e.g. the hospital the model was developed in) to a target population (e.g. a new hospital) whose event rates differ, while keeping the longitudinal sub-model unchanged.

The backward joint model factors the joint distribution as \(f(T, D \mid X)\, f(Y \mid T, D, X)\): the event-time model and the biomarker trajectory given the event time. Between populations it is often the first factor that changes most – a different case mix, standard of care, or referral pattern moves the event rates – while how a biomarker evolves in the years before an event is closer to biology and more stable. This is the label shift assumption of machine learning, and the backward factorization is exactly the one under which it is easy to act on: only survival_fit_all needs to change, and the result plugs into predictRisk, predictLongitudinal, simulateTrajectory, performancePlot and calibrationPlot with the source long_fit_all.

Three methods are available, by how much is known about the target:

"baseline"

Target outcomes are available (data_target, one row per subject). The hazard ratios are kept from the source and only the baseline cumulative hazard is re-estimated on the target (Breslow estimator with the source linear predictor as an offset). Needs few target events.

"recalibrate"

As "baseline", but the source linear predictor is also rescaled by a calibration slope \(\gamma\), estimated by a Cox model of the target outcome on the source linear predictor (\(\gamma < 1\): the source hazard ratios are too extreme for the target).

"unlabeled"

No target outcomes at all, only biomarker histories (data_predict_all). The target baseline cumulative hazard is taken to be the source one times \(e^{\alpha}\), and \(\alpha\) is estimated by maximizing the marginal likelihood of the target histories, $$\prod_i \int_{s_i}^{\infty} f(Y_i \mid T)\, f_\alpha(T \mid X_i)\, dT,$$ where \(s_i\) is the time up to which patient \(i\) is known to be event-free (by default their last measurement). Because \(f(Y \mid T)\) is held fixed, the shape of the target trajectories – how close they look to the trajectories of patients about to have an event – tells how far away the events are. This is the same integral predictRisk uses as its denominator, and it is only possible because the biomarker model conditions on the event time.

Usage

transportBJM(
  survival_fit_all,
  method = c("baseline", "recalibrate", "unlabeled"),
  data_target = NULL,
  update_event_type = FALSE,
  data_predict_all = NULL,
  long_fit_all = NULL,
  time_variable = NULL,
  survival_variable_all = NULL,
  survival_trans_function = NULL,
  landmark = NULL,
  data_source = NULL,
  cap_event_time = TRUE,
  n_grid = 200,
  upper = NULL,
  alpha_range = c(-4, 4)
)

Arguments

survival_fit_all

Output of survivalSub fit on the source data (right-censored, not stratified).

method

"baseline", "recalibrate" or "unlabeled"; see Description.

data_target

For "baseline" and "recalibrate": one row per target subject, with the outcome and covariates used in survival_fit_all$form_marginal_surv (and, with update_event_type = TRUE, form_conditional_cr).

update_event_type

For "baseline"/"recalibrate" with competing risks: also refit the event-type model on the target (default FALSE, keep the source one).

data_predict_all, long_fit_all, time_variable, survival_variable_all, survival_trans_function

For "unlabeled": the target biomarker histories and the source longitudinal sub-model, as for predictRisk. The event-time column may be absent or NA.

landmark

For "unlabeled": the time up to which each target patient is known to be event-free, a single number or a vector named by patient id. Defaults to each patient's last measurement time.

data_source

For "unlabeled": optionally, biomarker histories from the source population (in the format of data_predict_all). The shift is then estimated on them too, where it should be 0, and subtracted: whatever misfit of the model biases the estimate in the same way in both populations cancels. Recommended.

cap_event_time

For "unlabeled": if TRUE (default), an event time after the source follow-up is given the biomarker trajectory of an event at the end of follow-up, as in simulateTrajectory, instead of extrapolating the longitudinal sub-model.

n_grid, upper

For "unlabeled": the number of grid intervals on (0, upper] used for the integral, and the upper end of the grid (default three times the source follow-up); the probability of an event beyond upper is placed at upper.

alpha_range

For "unlabeled": the search interval for \(\alpha\), the log ratio of target to source baseline hazard.

Value

An object of class c("transportBJM", "survivalSub.BJM"): survival_fit_all with an extra element transport (the method, the target baseline cumulative hazard, the calibration slope, and alpha with its standard error for "unlabeled"). Use it in place of survival_fit_all anywhere in the package.

Details

Only the marginal event-time model is transported; the longitudinal sub-model, and by default the event-type model, are the source ones. If the biomarker trajectories before an event themselves differ between the populations (different assays, measurement schedules that depend on health), label shift does not hold and "unlabeled" is biased. "unlabeled" identifies a single proportional shift; it carries no information from patients without any measurement, and little from patients with only one.

Examples

data(pbc3)
first <- pbc3[!duplicated(pbc3$id), ]
odd <- seq_len(nrow(first)) %% 2 == 1
source <- first[!odd, ]
target <- first[odd, ]
fit_src <- survivalSub(source, Surv(years, status3) ~ age + sex, NULL)
fit_tgt <- transportBJM(fit_src, "baseline", data_target = target)
fit_tgt
